{"selected_source_ids":["D01","D02","D05","D06","D07","D09","D10","D11","D14","D15","D16","D17","D18","D19","D20"],"excluded_sources":[{"source_id":"D03","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D04","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D08","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D12","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D13","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"}],"selection_rationale":"The goal is to assemble primary, decision-relevant adsorption studies that (1) link PFAS structure to adsorption mechanisms and media properties, (2) quantify effects of water matrix constituents on performance, and (3) support conditional media-selection guidance rather than universal rankings.

Included studies
- D01 reports detailed batch and column experiments on anion exchange resins (AERs) with different functional groups and alkyl chain lengths, under drinking-water-relevant PFAS concentrations and matrices. It provides explicit data on selectivity versus PFAS chain length and functional group, plus competition from sulfate and humic acid—directly relevant to RT01-C1 and RT01-C2, and to conditional selection among AERs.
- D02 is a comparative experimental and cost analysis of GAC, ion exchange (IX), and a surface-modified organoclay across multiple water types. It explicitly evaluates how water quality and adsorbent use rate affect performance and cost, giving strong evidence for RT01-C2 and RT01-C3.
- D05 compares two novel carbonaceous adsorbents across multiple PFAS (varied chain length and functionality) with isotherms and textural characterization. It links pore structure and surface chemistry to PFAS adsorption trends, supporting RT01-C1 and providing complementary carbon-based media data.
- D06 compares PFAS removal by eight GACs and an alternative adsorbent across several groundwaters using RSSCTs and pilot data. It speaks directly to sorbent variability, water-quality impacts, and how to interpret lab tests for field media selection (RT01-C2 and RT01-C3).
- D07 evaluates "+green" sorption media for PFOS and PFOA with equilibrium and kinetic batch tests. While limited to two PFAS, it provides primary data on alternative adsorbents and helps illustrate how media properties affect PFAS sorption under relatively simple matrices (RT01-C1, partially RT01-C2).
- D09 investigates PFOA/PFOS removal by a strong-base IX resin under varying pH, DOM type/charge density, inorganic ions, and real water matrices. It provides detailed mechanistic and modeling evidence on organic matter and inorganic competition (RT01-C2) for IX media.
- D10 compares GAC, PAC, and ball-milled colloidal activated carbon for multiple PFAS, analyzing chain-length and functional-group effects, competition among PFAS, and the influence of ionic strength, pH, and humic acid. This strongly informs RT01-C1 and RT01-C2 for carbon-based media.
- D11 assesses a specialty biochar-containing adsorbent for PFAS removal from surface water. It quantifies how pH, TOC/DOC, and major cations/anions affect short- versus long-chain PFAS removal using response surface modeling and correlations, directly informing RT01-C2 and providing nuanced media–matrix interactions.
- D14 evaluates specialty adsorbents (CPS, ZIPGEM) in surface water for long- and short-chain PFAS under column conditions, comparing breakthrough, adsorption order, and suggesting candidate media for application. It supports RT01-C1 and provides comparative evidence for RT01-C3.
- D15 is a pilot study on RO/NF rejection of PFAS and sorption to treatment materials (including IX softening resin and filters). While not a classic adsorbent-treatment study, it provides primary data on chain-length and functional-group-dependent adsorption to ix-type and other surfaces in real groundwater, contributing to RT01-C1 and giving context on inadvertent adsorption in multi-barrier systems.
- D16 examines modified coal fly ash (CFA) for PFAS in landfill leachate, with mechanistic analysis (role of oxides, surface charge, hydrophobic interactions) and systematic tests across PFAS chain lengths and doses. It offers both structural-mechanistic insights (RT01-C1) and matrix-related behavior in a complex leachate (RT01-C2).
- D17 investigates sorption of a suite of PFAS and precursors on several GACs under realistic drinking-water conditions, emphasizing chain length, functional group, branching, and precursor structure. It directly addresses RT01-C1, including precursor behavior.
- D18 studies simultaneous removal of PFAS and Cd(II) with regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents across Milli-Q water, groundwater, and wastewaters, including DOM and co-contaminant effects and regeneration performance. It gives matrix- and co-contaminant-dependent adsorption behavior (RT01-C2) and practical considerations for media re-use.
- D19 analyzes short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal activated carbon as a function of ionic strength, inorganic anions, DOM of different molecular weights, and PFAS chain length/functional group. It contributes detailed mechanistic and matrix-effects data highly relevant to short-chain PFAS challenges (RT01-C1, RT01-C2).
- D20 uses RSSCTs to evaluate GAC and anion exchange resin (AIX) individually and in series for six PFAS under varied pH, conductivity, and organic carbon content in artificial groundwater. It directly links water quality and PFAS mixture to breakthrough behavior and compares sorbent classes, providing very strong evidence for RT01-C2 and structure-based, conditional media-selection logic (RT01-C3).

Excluded studies
- D03 is explicitly a review article on PFAS adsorption mechanisms and polymeric adsorbents, not a primary study (review_or_nonprimary).
- D04 is a review focused on regeneration, management, and sustainability of PFAS adsorbents, not primary experimental work (review_or_nonprimary).
- D08 focuses on VUV/sulfite-driven degradation (destructive treatment) and not on adsorption media, so it falls outside the adsorption-focused task (task_irrelevant).
- D12 is a health-burden versus benefit assessment of GAC treatment using LCA/risk concepts. It offers little extractable adsorption-performance detail relevant to media selection mechanisms or matrix effects (task_irrelevant for this specific review focus).
- D13 is a review article on PFAS sensor and sorbent selectivity rather than a primary experimental or modeling study (review_or_nonprimary).

The selected corpus spans multiple adsorbent classes (GAC, PAC, colloidal AC, biochar, AER/IX, specialty media, organoclays, CFA, CAC) and matrices (groundwater, surface water, drinking water, wastewater, leachate), providing complementary coverage of PFAS structural effects, matrix impacts, and comparative performance needed to support conditional media-selection criteria without claiming universal superiority of any one class.","component_coverage":[{"component_id":"RT01-C1","selected_source_ids":["D01","D05","D07","D10","D14","D16","D17","D18","D19","D15","D02","D06","D09","D11","D20"],"rationale":"Mechanistic and structure–property evidence is provided by multiple primary studies:
- D01 characterizes how AER properties (long alkyl chains, gel vs macroporous structure, strong-base quaternary amines) govern selectivity among multiple PFAS (including PFOS, PFOA, PFBA, 6:2 FTS), tying sorbent functional group and hydrophobicity to PFAS chain length and headgroup.
- D05 compares two novel carbonaceous materials, relating BET surface area, pore size distribution, and composition to isotherms for multiple PFAS (short- and long-chain PFCAs/PFSAs), giving explicit chain-length and functional-group-dependent adsorption sequences.
- D07 provides equilibrium and kinetic data for PFOS and PFOA on green media, illustrating how media composition and porosity affect adsorption of specific PFAS headgroups and similar chain length.
- D10 dissects PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, PFOS adsorption on GAC/PAC/colloidal AC, quantifying chain length and functional group effects, competition between PFAS, and linking sorption coefficients to log Kow.
- D14 compares long- vs short-chain PFAS removal patterns for specialty media (CPS, ZIPGEM) and offers observed adsorption orders (PFOS > PFOA > shorter chains), giving chain-length and functional-group-based selectivity insight.
- D16 uses modified CFA to study adsorption of PFBA–PFDoDA, explicitly testing how chain length and functional group interact with mineral surface chemistry and demonstrating differential uptake at varying adsorbent doses.
- D17 systematically examines PFCA (C4–C12), PFSA (C5–C10), and various precursors on three GACs, showing hydrophobic chain-length trends, sulfonate vs carboxylate effects, ether/sulfonamide linker impacts, and precursor behavior under drinking-water conditions.
- D18 includes multiple PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, GenX) on AC and biochar-based adsorbents, providing comparative sorption capacities and highlighting how GenX (short-chain ether PFAS) behaves differently from legacy PFAS.
- D19 focuses on short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal AC, with detailed analysis of how perfluorinated chain length, ether substitutions, and functional-group changes (PFCA vs PFSA) alter adsorption affinity.
- D15, though focused on membranes, provides chain-length- and headgroup-dependent sorption patterns onto IX softening resin and other solid-phase materials, adding complementary evidence on precursor and long-chain vs short-chain uptake.
- D02, D06, D09, D11, and D20 contribute comparative PFAS removal sequences for different sorbents (GAC vs IX vs specialty media) across PFAS profiles, reinforcing how chain length and headgroup govern media preference even when their primary emphasis is on matrix or performance metrics. Together these papers give strong empirical grounding for explaining adsorption mechanisms and material properties as a function of PFAS molecular structure and precursors."},{"component_id":"RT01-C2","selected_source_ids":["D01","D02","D06","D09","D10","D11","D16","D17","D18","D19","D20","D07","D14","D15"],"rationale":"Matrix and co-contaminant effects are extensively covered:
- D01 examines sulfate and humic acid (HA) effects on PFAS adsorption to AERs and compares pure water versus tap/drinking water, explicitly quantifying competition from inorganic anions and DOM at drinking-water-level PFAS concentrations.
- D02 evaluates GAC, IX, and organoclay across different real and synthetic waters, using adsorbent use rate and levelized media cost as metrics while highlighting how DOC, ionic constituents, and PFAS concentration alter breakthrough and economics.
- D06 uses RSSCT and pilot studies across multiple groundwaters, illustrating how DOC, co-contaminants (including VOCs in one case), and overall water quality impact PFAS breakthrough for various GACs and an alternative adsorbent.
- D09 systematically varies pH, SRNOM, different IHSS OM isolates, and inorganic ions in IX systems, quantifying how organic matter characteristics (charge density, MW) and competing anions influence PFOA/PFOS removal and modeling these interactions.
- D10 directly measures the impact of ionic strength, pH, and humic acid on PFAS adsorption to carbonaceous media, identifying when electrostatic vs hydrophobic interactions are more vulnerable to suppression.
- D11 uses response surface modeling and correlation analysis to quantify how pH, TOC/DOC, and multivalent cations (Ca, Mg, Fe, Al) correlate with changes in removal of multiple PFAS, clearly demonstrating matrix-dependent performance in surface water.
- D16 studies PFAS adsorption from landfill leachate on CFA, providing data under highly complex inorganic and organic backgrounds and exploring dose effects that interact with both PFAS structure and matrix composition.
- D17 is conducted under realistic drinking-water conditions rather than idealized lab waters, implicitly including NOM and background ions, and discusses how such constituents can influence sorption mechanisms.
- D18 compares Milli-Q, groundwater, and two wastewater matrices, showing that wastewater DOM and co-contaminants reduce PFAS uptake on AC and biochar and analyzing the combined effects of PFAS and Cd(II) concentration on isotherms.
- D19 systematically alters ionic strength/composition and DOM type (different MW distributions) to quantify their impact on short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal AC, directly addressing groundwater solute effects.
- D20 varies pH, conductivity (ionic strength), and organic carbon in artificial groundwater while tracking breakthrough for six PFAS on GAC, AIX, and combined configurations, giving a clear semi-factorial picture of matrix impacts and PFAS competition.
- D07 and D14, although less exhaustive on matrix factors, still inform how relatively simple matrices and native surface water constituents affect performance of alternative/specialty media.
- D15, by examining sorption to treatment materials under full-scale-like groundwater conditions, adds context on how realistic groundwater solutes influence PFAS accumulation on IX and membrane surfaces. Collectively these sources provide robust evidence on how DOM, inorganic ions, pH, competing contaminants, and influent concentration shape PFAS adsorption performance."},{"component_id":"RT01-C3","selected_source_ids":["D02","D06","D14","D20","D01","D10","D11","D18","D19"],"rationale":"Several selected studies move beyond isolated performance metrics to comparative, context-dependent insights that support conditional media-selection criteria:
- D02 explicitly frames its work as "PFAS adsorbent selection," comparing GAC, IX, and a surface-modified organoclay in terms of adsorbent use rate, water quality, and cost. It provides quantitative guidance on when IX versus GAC versus novel media are more practical, contingent on PFAS type, concentration, and matrix.
- D06 compares eight GACs and an alternative adsorbent across multiple groundwaters using RSSCTs and pilot data and discusses how predicted media life at selected breakthrough levels should inform sorbent choice and changeout strategy, rather than ranking media universally.
- D14 compares two specialty media for long- and short-chain PFAS removal from surface water, discusses their suitability as pretreatment to extend life of other advanced processes, and notes that media choice depends on target PFAS profile and desired effluent quality.
- D20 performs semi-factorial RSSCTs with GAC and AIX (alone and combined) under varying pH, conductivity, and organic carbon, concluding that the most effective sorbent or sorbent combination depends on site-specific water quality and PFAS mixture. It is directly framed to inform sorbent selection for groundwater remediation.
- D01, though focused on AERs, derives structure–property relationships (e.g., long alkyl chains, gel-type structure, strong-base groups) and links them to performance at low PFAS concentrations, supporting criteria for choosing among different IX formulations for specific PFAS and matrices.
- D10 contrasts GAC, PAC, and colloidal AC performance across PFAS types and environmental conditions, highlighting trade-offs in kinetics, capacity, and susceptibility to ionic strength and NOM—useful for specifying carbon form and operating regime rather than assuming one carbon type is always best.
- D11, through response surface modeling, identifies ranges of pH and TOC/DOC where the specialty adsorbent maintains good removal for different PFAS, helping define conditions under which such media are advantageous or disadvantaged relative to alternatives.
- D18 discusses how performance in wastewater versus cleaner matrices, plus adsorbent regenerability and mixed-contaminant handling (PFAS + Cd), should influence the selection and deployment of regenerable AC and biochar materials.
- D19 emphasizes that short-chain PFAS and high ionic strength/DOM create challenges for in situ CAC barriers and suggests that barrier design and media choice must reflect local groundwater solute composition and PFAS profile. Together these studies enable the review to formulate conditional, matrix- and PFAS-profile-dependent media-selection guidance and to avoid any universal claims of superiority for a single adsorbent class."}]}

You are selecting primary PFAS treatment studies for a focused professional
review. You receive one task and an anonymized, BGE-ranked list of candidate
document cards.

Classify every candidate card. Select every document that is an independent
primary study, is directly relevant to at least one task component, and
contains extractable decision-relevant evidence. There is no target number of
selected documents and no penalty for retaining all eligible studies.

Eligible evidence includes:

- primary experiments, pilot or field deployments, and quantitative modeling
  or life-cycle studies;
- complementary matrices, PFAS scopes, operating regimes, endpoints, and
  scales;
- documents with concrete methods, conditions, results, limitations, residuals,
  energy, or cost evidence; and
- evidence that permits meaningful comparison or explains non-comparability.

Do not select a document merely because its title repeats task words. Do not
select reviews, perspectives, reference lists, duplicate records, or the
held-out defining review. Do not exclude an otherwise eligible study merely
because another selected study reports similar findings. Do not infer facts
absent from a card. Selection is document-level only: do not write the review
and do not score candidate answers.

Every candidate source_id must appear exactly once, either in
selected_source_ids or excluded_sources. Each required component must be
covered by at least one selected source. Return selected_source_ids in BGE rank
order.

Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

component_coverage.rationale:
Mechanistic and structure–property evidence is provided by multiple primary studies:
- D01 characterizes how AER properties (long alkyl chains, gel vs macroporous structure, strong-base quaternary amines) govern selectivity among multiple PFAS (including PFOS, PFOA, PFBA, 6:2 FTS), tying sorbent functional group and hydrophobicity to PFAS chain length and headgroup.
- D05 compares two novel carbonaceous materials, relating BET surface area, pore size distribution, and composition to isotherms for multiple PFAS (short- and long-chain PFCAs/PFSAs), giving explicit chain-length and functional-group-dependent adsorption sequences.
- D07 provides equilibrium and kinetic data for PFOS and PFOA on green media, illustrating how media composition and porosity affect adsorption of specific PFAS headgroups and similar chain length.
- D10 dissects PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, PFOS adsorption on GAC/PAC/colloidal AC, quantifying chain length and functional group effects, competition between PFAS, and linking sorption coefficients to log Kow.
- D14 compares long- vs short-chain PFAS removal patterns for specialty media (CPS, ZIPGEM) and offers observed adsorption orders (PFOS > PFOA > shorter chains), giving chain-length and functional-group-based selectivity insight.
- D16 uses modified CFA to study adsorption of PFBA–PFDoDA, explicitly testing how chain length and functional group interact with mineral surface chemistry and demonstrating differential uptake at varying adsorbent doses.
- D17 systematically examines PFCA (C4–C12), PFSA (C5–C10), and various precursors on three GACs, showing hydrophobic chain-length trends, sulfonate vs carboxylate effects, ether/sulfonamide linker impacts, and precursor behavior under drinking-water conditions.
- D18 includes multiple PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, GenX) on AC and biochar-based adsorbents, providing comparative sorption capacities and highlighting how GenX (short-chain ether PFAS) behaves differently from legacy PFAS.
- D19 focuses on short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal AC, with detailed analysis of how perfluorinated chain length, ether substitutions, and functional-group changes (PFCA vs PFSA) alter adsorption affinity.
- D15, though focused on membranes, provides chain-length- and headgroup-dependent sorption patterns onto IX softening resin and other solid-phase materials, adding complementary evidence on precursor and long-chain vs short-chain uptake.
- D02, D06, D09, D11, and D20 contribute comparative PFAS removal sequences for different sorbents (GAC vs IX vs specialty media) across PFAS profiles, reinforcing how chain length and headgroup govern media preference even when their primary emphasis is on matrix or performance metrics. Together these papers give strong empirical grounding for explaining adsorption mechanisms and material properties as a function of PFAS molecular structure and precursors.

Matrix and co-contaminant effects are extensively covered:
- D01 examines sulfate and humic acid (HA) effects on PFAS adsorption to AERs and compares pure water versus tap/drinking water, explicitly quantifying competition from inorganic anions and DOM at drinking-water-level PFAS concentrations.
- D02 evaluates GAC, IX, and organoclay across different real and synthetic waters, using adsorbent use rate and levelized media cost as metrics while highlighting how DOC, ionic constituents, and PFAS concentration alter breakthrough and economics.
- D06 uses RSSCT and pilot studies across multiple groundwaters, illustrating how DOC, co-contaminants (including VOCs in one case), and overall water quality impact PFAS breakthrough for various GACs and an alternative adsorbent.
- D09 systematically varies pH, SRNOM, different IHSS OM isolates, and inorganic ions in IX systems, quantifying how organic matter characteristics (charge density, MW) and competing anions influence PFOA/PFOS removal and modeling these interactions.
- D10 directly measures the impact of ionic strength, pH, and humic acid on PFAS adsorption to carbonaceous media, identifying when electrostatic vs hydrophobic interactions are more vulnerable to suppression.
- D11 uses response surface modeling and correlation analysis to quantify how pH, TOC/DOC, and multivalent cations (Ca, Mg, Fe, Al) correlate with changes in removal of multiple PFAS, clearly demonstrating matrix-dependent performance in surface water.
- D16 studies PFAS adsorption from landfill leachate on CFA, providing data under highly complex inorganic and organic backgrounds and exploring dose effects that interact with both PFAS structure and matrix composition.
- D17 is conducted under realistic drinking-water conditions rather than idealized lab waters, implicitly including NOM and background ions, and discusses how such constituents can influence sorption mechanisms.
- D18 compares Milli-Q, groundwater, and two wastewater matrices, showing that wastewater DOM and co-contaminants reduce PFAS uptake on AC and biochar and analyzing the combined effects of PFAS and Cd(II) concentration on isotherms.
- D19 systematically alters ionic strength/composition and DOM type (different MW distributions) to quantify their impact on short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal AC, directly addressing groundwater solute effects.
- D20 varies pH, conductivity (ionic strength), and organic carbon in artificial groundwater while tracking breakthrough for six PFAS on GAC, AIX, and combined configurations, giving a clear semi-factorial picture of matrix impacts and PFAS competition.
- D07 and D14, although less exhaustive on matrix factors, still inform how relatively simple matrices and native surface water constituents affect performance of alternative/specialty media.
- D15, by examining sorption to treatment materials under full-scale-like groundwater conditions, adds context on how realistic groundwater solutes influence PFAS accumulation on IX and membrane surfaces. Collectively these sources provide robust evidence on how DOM, inorganic ions, pH, competing contaminants, and influent concentration shape PFAS adsorption performance.

Several selected studies move beyond isolated performance metrics to comparative, context-dependent insights that support conditional media-selection criteria:
- D02 explicitly frames its work as "PFAS adsorbent selection," comparing GAC, IX, and a surface-modified organoclay in terms of adsorbent use rate, water quality, and cost. It provides quantitative guidance on when IX versus GAC versus novel media are more practical, contingent on PFAS type, concentration, and matrix.
- D06 compares eight GACs and an alternative adsorbent across multiple groundwaters using RSSCTs and pilot data and discusses how predicted media life at selected breakthrough levels should inform sorbent choice and changeout strategy, rather than ranking media universally.
- D14 compares two specialty media for long- and short-chain PFAS removal from surface water, discusses their suitability as pretreatment to extend life of other advanced processes, and notes that media choice depends on target PFAS profile and desired effluent quality.
- D20 performs semi-factorial RSSCTs with GAC and AIX (alone and combined) under varying pH, conductivity, and organic carbon, concluding that the most effective sorbent or sorbent combination depends on site-specific water quality and PFAS mixture. It is directly framed to inform sorbent selection for groundwater remediation.
- D01, though focused on AERs, derives structure–property relationships (e.g., long alkyl chains, gel-type structure, strong-base groups) and links them to performance at low PFAS concentrations, supporting criteria for choosing among different IX formulations for specific PFAS and matrices.
- D10 contrasts GAC, PAC, and colloidal AC performance across PFAS types and environmental conditions, highlighting trade-offs in kinetics, capacity, and susceptibility to ionic strength and NOM—useful for specifying carbon form and operating regime rather than assuming one carbon type is always best.
- D11, through response surface modeling, identifies ranges of pH and TOC/DOC where the specialty adsorbent maintains good removal for different PFAS, helping define conditions under which such media are advantageous or disadvantaged relative to alternatives.
- D18 discusses how performance in wastewater versus cleaner matrices, plus adsorbent regenerability and mixed-contaminant handling (PFAS + Cd), should influence the selection and deployment of regenerable AC and biochar materials.
- D19 emphasizes that short-chain PFAS and high ionic strength/DOM create challenges for in situ CAC barriers and suggests that barrier design and media choice must reflect local groundwater solute composition and PFAS profile. Together these studies enable the review to formulate conditional, matrix- and PFAS-profile-dependent media-selection guidance and to avoid any universal claims of superiority for a single adsorbent class.

result.selection_rationale:
The goal is to assemble primary, decision-relevant adsorption studies that (1) link PFAS structure to adsorption mechanisms and media properties, (2) quantify effects of water matrix constituents on performance, and (3) support conditional media-selection guidance rather than universal rankings.

Included studies
- D01 reports detailed batch and column experiments on anion exchange resins (AERs) with different functional groups and alkyl chain lengths, under drinking-water-relevant PFAS concentrations and matrices. It provides explicit data on selectivity versus PFAS chain length and functional group, plus competition from sulfate and humic acid—directly relevant to RT01-C1 and RT01-C2, and to conditional selection among AERs.
- D02 is a comparative experimental and cost analysis of GAC, ion exchange (IX), and a surface-modified organoclay across multiple water types. It explicitly evaluates how water quality and adsorbent use rate affect performance and cost, giving strong evidence for RT01-C2 and RT01-C3.
- D05 compares two novel carbonaceous adsorbents across multiple PFAS (varied chain length and functionality) with isotherms and textural characterization. It links pore structure and surface chemistry to PFAS adsorption trends, supporting RT01-C1 and providing complementary carbon-based media data.
- D06 compares PFAS removal by eight GACs and an alternative adsorbent across several groundwaters using RSSCTs and pilot data. It speaks directly to sorbent variability, water-quality impacts, and how to interpret lab tests for field media selection (RT01-C2 and RT01-C3).
- D07 evaluates "+green" sorption media for PFOS and PFOA with equilibrium and kinetic batch tests. While limited to two PFAS, it provides primary data on alternative adsorbents and helps illustrate how media properties affect PFAS sorption under relatively simple matrices (RT01-C1, partially RT01-C2).
- D09 investigates PFOA/PFOS removal by a strong-base IX resin under varying pH, DOM type/charge density, inorganic ions, and real water matrices. It provides detailed mechanistic and modeling evidence on organic matter and inorganic competition (RT01-C2) for IX media.
- D10 compares GAC, PAC, and ball-milled colloidal activated carbon for multiple PFAS, analyzing chain-length and functional-group effects, competition among PFAS, and the influence of ionic strength, pH, and humic acid. This strongly informs RT01-C1 and RT01-C2 for carbon-based media.
- D11 assesses a specialty biochar-containing adsorbent for PFAS removal from surface water. It quantifies how pH, TOC/DOC, and major cations/anions affect short- versus long-chain PFAS removal using response surface modeling and correlations, directly informing RT01-C2 and providing nuanced media–matrix interactions.
- D14 evaluates specialty adsorbents (CPS, ZIPGEM) in surface water for long- and short-chain PFAS under column conditions, comparing breakthrough, adsorption order, and suggesting candidate media for application. It supports RT01-C1 and provides comparative evidence for RT01-C3.
- D15 is a pilot study on RO/NF rejection of PFAS and sorption to treatment materials (including IX softening resin and filters). While not a classic adsorbent-treatment study, it provides primary data on chain-length and functional-group-dependent adsorption to ix-type and other surfaces in real groundwater, contributing to RT01-C1 and giving context on inadvertent adsorption in multi-barrier systems.
- D16 examines modified coal fly ash (CFA) for PFAS in landfill leachate, with mechanistic analysis (role of oxides, surface charge, hydrophobic interactions) and systematic tests across PFAS chain lengths and doses. It offers both structural-mechanistic insights (RT01-C1) and matrix-related behavior in a complex leachate (RT01-C2).
- D17 investigates sorption of a suite of PFAS and precursors on several GACs under realistic drinking-water conditions, emphasizing chain length, functional group, branching, and precursor structure. It directly addresses RT01-C1, including precursor behavior.
- D18 studies simultaneous removal of PFAS and Cd(II) with regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents across Milli-Q water, groundwater, and wastewaters, including DOM and co-contaminant effects and regeneration performance. It gives matrix- and co-contaminant-dependent adsorption behavior (RT01-C2) and practical considerations for media re-use.
- D19 analyzes short-chain PFAA adsorption to colloidal activated carbon as a function of ionic strength, inorganic anions, DOM of different molecular weights, and PFAS chain length/functional group. It contributes detailed mechanistic and matrix-effects data highly relevant to short-chain PFAS challenges (RT01-C1, RT01-C2).
- D20 uses RSSCTs to evaluate GAC and anion exchange resin (AIX) individually and in series for six PFAS under varied pH, conductivity, and organic carbon content in artificial groundwater. It directly links water quality and PFAS mixture to breakthrough behavior and compares sorbent classes, providing very strong evidence for RT01-C2 and structure-based, conditional media-selection logic (RT01-C3).

Excluded studies
- D03 is explicitly a review article on PFAS adsorption mechanisms and polymeric adsorbents, not a primary study (review_or_nonprimary).
- D04 is a review focused on regeneration, management, and sustainability of PFAS adsorbents, not primary experimental work (review_or_nonprimary).
- D08 focuses on VUV/sulfite-driven degradation (destructive treatment) and not on adsorption media, so it falls outside the adsorption-focused task (task_irrelevant).
- D12 is a health-burden versus benefit assessment of GAC treatment using LCA/risk concepts. It offers little extractable adsorption-performance detail relevant to media selection mechanisms or matrix effects (task_irrelevant for this specific review focus).
- D13 is a review article on PFAS sensor and sorbent selectivity rather than a primary experimental or modeling study (review_or_nonprimary).

The selected corpus spans multiple adsorbent classes (GAC, PAC, colloidal AC, biochar, AER/IX, specialty media, organoclays, CFA, CAC) and matrices (groundwater, surface water, drinking water, wastewater, leachate), providing complementary coverage of PFAS structural effects, matrix impacts, and comparative performance needed to support conditional media-selection criteria without claiming universal superiority of any one class.
